overview.text: The spinal cord is a single structure, whereas the adult brain is described in terms of four major regions: the cerebrum, the diencephalon, the brain stem, and the cerebellum.
overview.label: 13.2 The Central Nervous System

overview.text: The wrinkled portion is the cerebral cortex, and the rest of the structure is beneath that outer covering.
overview.label: 13.2 The Cerebrum

overview.text: It separates the cerebrum into two distinct halves, a right and left cerebral hemisphere.
overview.label: 13.2 The Cerebrum

overview.text: Deep within the cerebrum, the white matter of the corpus callosum provides the major pathway for communication between the two hemispheres of the cerebral cortex.
overview.label: 13.2 The Cerebrum

cortex.text: The cerebrum is covered by a continuous layer of gray matter that wraps around either side of the forebrain—the cerebral cortex.
cortex.label: 13.2 Cerebral Cortex

cortex.text: A gyrus (plural = gyri) is the ridge of one of those wrinkles, and a sulcus (plural = sulci) is the groove between two gyri.
cortex.label: 13.2 Cerebral Cortex

cortex.text: The pattern of these folds of tissue indicates specific regions of the cerebral cortex.
cortex.label: 13.2 Cerebral Cortex

cortex.text: Superior to the lateral sulcus are the parietal lobe and frontal lobe, which are separated from each other by the central sulcus.
cortex.label: 13.2 Cerebral Cortex

cortex.text: The posterior region of the cortex is the occipital lobe, which has no obvious anatomical border between it and the parietal or temporal lobes on the lateral surface of the brain.
cortex.label: 13.2 Cerebral Cortex

precentral.text: Anterior to the central sulcus is the frontal lobe, which is primarily associated with motor functions.
precentral.label: 13.2 Cerebral Cortex

precentral.text: The precentral gyrus is the primary motor cortex.
precentral.label: 13.2 Cerebral Cortex

postcentral.text: The main sensation associated with the parietal lobe is somatosensation, meaning the general sensations associated with the body.
postcentral.label: 13.2 Cerebral Cortex

postcentral.text: Posterior to the central sulcus is the postcentral gyrus, the primary somatosensory cortex, which is identified as Brodmann’s areas 1, 2, and 3.
postcentral.label: 13.2 Cerebral Cortex

occipital.text: The posterior region of the cortex is the occipital lobe, which has no obvious anatomical border between it and the parietal or temporal lobes on the lateral surface of the brain.
occipital.label: 13.2 Cerebral Cortex

occipital.text: Areas 17 and 18 in the occipital lobe are responsible for primary visual perception.
occipital.label: 13.2 Cerebral Cortex

suptemporal.text: The temporal lobe is associated with primary auditory sensation, known as Brodmann’s areas 41 and 42 in the superior temporal lobe.
suptemporal.label: 13.2 Cerebral Cortex

white.text: Deep within the cerebrum, the white matter of the corpus callosum provides the major pathway for communication between the two hemispheres of the cerebral cortex.
white.label: 13.2 The Cerebrum

basal.text: The basal nuclei are a set of nuclei in the cerebrum responsible for comparing cortical processing with the general state of activity in the nervous system to influence the likelihood of movement taking place.
basal.label: 13.2 Subcortical structures

basal.text: The major structures of the basal nuclei that control movement are the caudate, putamen, and globus pallidus, which are located deep in the cerebrum.
basal.label: 13.2 Subcortical structures

caudate.text: The major structures of the basal nuclei that control movement are the caudate, putamen, and globus pallidus, which are located deep in the cerebrum.
caudate.label: 13.2 Subcortical structures

caudate.text: The caudate is a long nucleus that follows the basic C-shape of the cerebrum from the frontal lobe, through the parietal and occipital lobes, into the temporal lobe.
caudate.label: 13.2 Subcortical structures

caudate.text: Together, the caudate and putamen are called the striatum.
caudate.label: 13.2 Subcortical structures

putamen.text: The major structures of the basal nuclei that control movement are the caudate, putamen, and globus pallidus, which are located deep in the cerebrum.
putamen.label: 13.2 Subcortical structures

putamen.text: The putamen is mostly deep in the anterior regions of the frontal and parietal lobes.
putamen.label: 13.2 Subcortical structures

putamen.text: Together, the caudate and putamen are called the striatum.
putamen.label: 13.2 Subcortical structures

pallidus.text: The major structures of the basal nuclei that control movement are the caudate, putamen, and globus pallidus, which are located deep in the cerebrum.
pallidus.label: 13.2 Subcortical structures

pallidus.text: The globus pallidus is a layered nucleus that lies just medial to the putamen; they are called the lenticular nuclei because they look like curved pieces fitting together like lenses.
pallidus.label: 13.2 Subcortical structures

pallidus.text: The globus pallidus has two subdivisions, the external and internal segments, which are lateral and medial, respectively.
pallidus.label: 13.2 Subcortical structures

hippo.text: The hippocampus and amygdala are medial-lobe structures that, along with the adjacent cortex, are involved in long-term memory formation and emotional responses.
hippo.label: 13.2 Subcortical structures

dien.text: The diencephalon is deep beneath the cerebrum and constitutes the walls of the third ventricle.
dien.label: 13.2 The Diencephalon

dien.text: The diencephalon can be described as any region of the brain with “thalamus” in its name.
dien.label: 13.2 The Diencephalon

thalamus.text: The thalamus is a collection of nuclei that relay information between the cerebral cortex and the periphery, spinal cord, or brain stem.
thalamus.label: 13.2 Thalamus

thalamus.text: All sensory information, except for the sense of smell, passes through the thalamus before processing by the cortex.
thalamus.label: 13.2 Thalamus

hypothalamus.text: Inferior and slightly anterior to the thalamus is the hypothalamus, the other major region of the diencephalon.
hypothalamus.label: 13.2 Hypothalamus

hypothalamus.text: The hypothalamus is a collection of nuclei that are largely involved in regulating homeostasis.
hypothalamus.label: 13.2 Hypothalamus

hypothalamus.text: The hypothalamus is the executive region in charge of the autonomic nervous system and the endocrine system through its regulation of the anterior pituitary gland.
hypothalamus.label: 13.2 Hypothalamus

pineal.text: There are other structures, such as the epithalamus, which contains the pineal gland, or the subthalamus, which includes the subthalamic nucleus that is part of the basal nuclei.
pineal.label: 13.2 The Diencephalon

brainstem.text: The structure emerges from the ventral surface of the forebrain as a tapering cone that connects the brain to the spinal cord.
brainstem.label: 13.2 Brain Stem

brainstem.text: The midbrain coordinates sensory representations of the visual, auditory, and somatosensory perceptual spaces.
brainstem.label: 13.2 Brain Stem

brainstem.text: The pons and the medulla regulate several crucial functions, including the cardiovascular and respiratory systems and rates.
brainstem.label: 13.2 Brain Stem

midbrain.text: One of the original regions of the embryonic brain, the midbrain is a small region between the thalamus and pons.
midbrain.label: 13.2 Midbrain

midbrain.text: The cerebral aqueduct passes through the center of the midbrain, such that these regions are the roof and floor of that canal.
midbrain.label: 13.2 Midbrain

inferiorcoll.text: The tectum is composed of four bumps known as the colliculi (singular = colliculus), which means “little hill” in Latin.
inferiorcoll.label: 13.2 Midbrain

inferiorcoll.text: The inferior colliculus is the inferior pair of these enlargements and is part of the auditory brain stem pathway.
inferiorcoll.label: 13.2 Midbrain

superiorcoll.text: The tectum is composed of four bumps known as the colliculi (singular = colliculus), which means “little hill” in Latin.
superiorcoll.label: 13.2 Midbrain

superiorcoll.text: The superior colliculus is the superior pair and combines sensory information about visual space, auditory space, and somatosensory space.
superiorcoll.label: 13.2 Midbrain

pons.text: The word pons comes from the Latin word for bridge.
pons.label: 13.2 Pons

pons.text: It is visible on the anterior surface of the brain stem as the thick bundle of white matter attached to the cerebellum.
pons.label: 13.2 Pons

pons.text: The pons is the main connection between the cerebellum and the brain stem.
pons.label: 13.2 Pons

medulla.text: The medulla is the region known as the myelencephalon in the embryonic brain.
medulla.label: 13.2 Medulla

medulla.text: The initial portion of the name, “myel,” refers to the significant white matter found in this region—especially on its exterior, which is continuous with the white matter of the spinal cord.
medulla.label: 13.2 Medulla

cerebellum.text: The cerebellum, as the name suggests, is the “little brain.”
cerebellum.label: 13.2 The Cerebellum

cerebellum.text: The cerebellum is largely responsible for comparing information from the cerebrum with sensory feedback from the periphery through the spinal cord.
cerebellum.label: 13.2 The Cerebellum

cerebellum.text: It accounts for approximately 10 percent of the mass of the brain.
cerebellum.label: 13.2 The Cerebellum

lateralv.text: There are four ventricles within the brain, all of which developed from the original hollow space within the neural tube, the central canal.
lateralv.label: 13.3 The Ventricles

lateralv.text: The first two are named the lateral ventricles and are deep within the cerebrum.
lateralv.label: 13.3 The Ventricles

ivf.text: These ventricles are connected to the third ventricle by two openings called the interventricular foramina.
ivf.label: 13.3 The Ventricles

ivf.text: The interventricular foramina connect the frontal region of the lateral ventricles with the third ventricle.
ivf.label: 13.3 The Ventricles

thirdv.text: The third ventricle is the space between the left and right sides of the diencephalon, which opens into the cerebral aqueduct that passes through the midbrain.
thirdv.label: 13.3 The Ventricles

thirdv.text: The third ventricle is the space bounded by the medial walls of the hypothalamus and thalamus.
thirdv.label: 13.3 The Ventricles

aqueduct.text: The cerebral aqueduct opens just inferior to the epithalamus and passes through the midbrain.
aqueduct.label: 13.3 The Ventricles

aqueduct.text: The tectum and tegmentum of the midbrain are the roof and floor of the cerebral aqueduct, respectively.
aqueduct.label: 13.3 The Ventricles

fourthv.text: The aqueduct opens up into the fourth ventricle.
fourthv.label: 13.3 The Ventricles

fourthv.text: The floor of the fourth ventricle is the dorsal surface of the pons and upper medulla (that gray matter making a continuation of the tegmentum of the midbrain).
fourthv.label: 13.3 The Ventricles

fourthv.text: The fourth ventricle then narrows into the central canal of the spinal cord.
fourthv.label: 13.3 The Ventricles

canal.text: The fourth ventricle then narrows into the central canal of the spinal cord.
canal.label: 13.3 The Ventricles

choroid.text: In some of these spaces, CSF is produced by filtering of the blood that is performed by a specialized membrane known as a choroid plexus.
choroid.label: 13.3 The Ventricular System

choroid.text: The choroid plexuses are found in all four ventricles.
choroid.label: 13.3 Cerebrospinal Fluid Circulation

pituitary.text: The hypothalamus is the executive region in charge of the autonomic nervous system and the endocrine system through its regulation of the anterior pituitary gland.
pituitary.label: 13.2 Hypothalamus
